segments.original: After the collapse of the Eastern Bloc, Europe entered the 1990s fueled by, among other things, a spirit of artistic freedom. But the economic cost of change was reflected in budget constraints on film production in some countries, limiting costly period dramas to those countries that already had a long track record in the genre.

segments.original: The decade began with Jean-Paul Rappeneau's (b. 1932) dazzling adaptation of Cyrano de Bergerac (1990). segments.original: "Buongiorno Principessa!" Rarely has an expression taken from an Italian film become so well known in every corner of the world. And when it is spoken with arms flung wide by a child leaping out of a cupboard with the burst of joy we see in Guido and Dora's son... it melts anyone's heart. The film from which we borrowed the memory of this scene, as everyone knows, is Life Is Beautiful (1997), and it put actor, director and screenwriter Roberto Benigni in the international spotlight.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The attention Life Is Beautiful drew is explained not only by the many awards it won in Europe and, above all, in Hollywood, but also by the debate it reignited (after Schindler's List (1993)) about the possibilities and limits of representing the Holocaust. The main reason for any controversy was precisely what defines this filmmaker's work: comedy. The Holocaust, it was argued, could not be viewed that way. Benigni reacted to this without bitterness, as can be seen in his answer in a 1999 interview with The Guardian: "We clowns need to be mistreated. It keeps us alive, real. Only a genius like Fellini knew how to do that. He saw clowns as benefactors, saints, as the epitome of tragedy." This same personality that shrugged off bad reviews is the personality of Guido, the protagonist of Life Is Beautiful, played by Benigni, who bursts into the film with infectious enthusiasm. We know it won't all be roses, because the opening line serves as a warning: "This is a simple story, but not an easy one to tell. Like a fable, there is sorrow, and like a fable, it is full of wonder and happiness."

tracks.title: Learn more: A Fable of Love and Survival (2)

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Roberto Benigni's reasons for making this film were neither political nor historical, although he and screenwriter Vincenzo Cerami (b. 1940) took the precaution of hiring consultants from the Center for Jewish Documentation in Milan and holding screenings for groups of Italian Jews before the release. His desire to tell a story of love and humanity in an extreme context needed only this, so to speak, scientific confirmation to launch into international distribution. And its success was confirmed in Cannes, Warsaw, the United States and even Jerusalem, where the film later won the "Best Jewish Experience" award at the Jerusalem Film Festival. The great human inspiration behind Life Is Beautiful was Rubino Romeo Salmonì (1920-2011). It was the story of this Italian Jew, captured by the Nazis in 1943, that caught Benigni's attention through the book Ho sconfitto Hitler (literally, I Defeated Hitler), in which he recounts how he survived Auschwitz. Before putting it into writing, Rubino shared his experience with children and teenagers, doing so in a more optimistic way, as the book reveals, adopting a tone of a certain irony. And it was this man's strong, confident spirit (one that never forgot comedy) that suggested the possibility of talking about love in the most catastrophic of situations. It is no accident that the film's seemingly trivial title also has a very specific origin: it was taken from the sentence with which Leon Trotsky ended his testament, written in Mexico: "Life is beautiful. Let the future generations cleanse it of all evil, oppression and violence, and enjoy it to the full."

segments.original: Kenneth Branagh (b. 1960) followed up his blood-and-mud version of Henry V (1989) with Much Ado About Nothing (1993), the best Shakespeare adaptation of the decade, with the exception of Baz Luhrmann's (b. 1962) brilliant take on Romeo + Juliet (1996). Branagh's Hamlet (1996), however, the first to use Shakespeare's complete text, was only a partial success. Shakespeare in Love (1998), co-written by playwright Tom Stoppard (b. 1937), proved even more popular, captivating audiences and winning the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay. Derek Jarman (1942-1994) produced one of his finest works in 1991, an adaptation of another Elizabethan drama, Christopher Marlowe's Edward II.

segments.original: The most important Spanish period film of the decade was the Oscar-winning Belle époque (1992). La lengua de las mariposas (Butterfly, 1999) and Ken Loach's (b. 1936) Land and Freedom (1995) focused on the Spanish Civil War, while Vacas (Cows, 1992) told the eccentric story of a Basque family over seven decades. A similar narrative structure was adopted by Hungarian director István Szabó (b. 1938) in Sunshine (1999), and with even better results by the Greek Theo Angelopoulos (b. 1935) in To Vlemma tou Odyssea (Ulysses' Gaze, 1995).

segments.original: Il postino (The Postman, 1994), a fictional account of the meeting between Pablo Neruda and a lovestruck postman, was one of the most internationally successful Italian productions, though it was soon overshadowed by La vita è bella (Life Is Beautiful, 1997), directed by and starring Roberto Benigni (b. 1952). The comedy-drama, set mostly in a concentration camp, was one of the decade's biggest period-film hits, although opinions on its merits remain divided.
